title: The wars
hook: France's religious wars raged around his tower, and he talked peace to both sides

segments.voice: Yesterday, the daughters: one passing sentence that readers still wonder about. Your line was hidden grief. Who did you go a little gentler with? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-five.

A country house in France. Outside, armed bands from two sides of a civil war over religion ride the roads. Neighbors bar their gates, hire guards, and sleep badly. One house leaves its gate open. Inside, in a tower, a man is writing a book about himself. He belongs to one of the two churches and doesn't hide it. And men on both sides use him to carry word between them. Today, how Montaigne lived in the middle of a war about faith.
screen: `A CIVIL WAR OVER RELIGION.` → `ONE GATE LEFT OPEN.` → `WORD CARRIED BETWEEN THEM.`

segments.voice: First, the open gate. Montaigne writes that while others fortified their homes, he kept his unguarded, with only a porter at the door, more for old custom and ceremony than for defense. A guarded house, he reasons, invites attack, because it looks like a prize. His stayed open, and he says it was spared. Second, how he talked. In the essay Of the useful and the honest, he describes going between great men on opposite sides. He tells each one plainly what he'd tell the other, and he doesn't pretend to belong to the side he doesn't. Because he wasn't playing a game, he says, people trusted him with their real thoughts. Third, his candle. He says he would gladly carry a candle to Saint Michael and another to his dragon. It's a joke with an edge, and he tells it against himself: he'll follow his own side, he says, even to the fire, but not into it if he can help it. Fourth, the cost. In a later essay he admits that moderation got him beaten from every side. To one camp he looked like the enemy, to the other camp the same. Talking to both doesn't make everyone love you. Often it makes both suspicious. He did it anyway, out loud, in his own name. Closer to home, the war is smaller: two siblings, two coworkers, two friends who stopped speaking. Montaigne's way isn't pretending they agree. It's keeping the gate open and saying the same true thing in both rooms.
screen: `AN OPEN GATE, A LONE PORTER.` · `THE SAME WORDS TO EACH SIDE.` · `A CANDLE FOR THE SAINT AND DRAGON.` · `SUSPECTED BY BOTH.` · then, large: `TALK TO BOTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: talk to both sides of one quarrel, first in your head. Sit, and breathe slowly. Pick a small quarrel you're near, not necessarily in. Picture the first person and, silently, say one true thing you'd be willing to say to them. Now picture the second person. Say the same true thing to them. Notice where the words wanted to change, to flatter one side or cut the other. Keep them the same. The bell holds the time.
The wars. France's wars of religion, which Montaigne lived through with his gate open, saying the same plain words to both sides. Today's word.
Your line: talk to both. Today, in one disagreement near you, say nothing to one side you wouldn't say to the other. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: Montaigne describes keeping his house unguarded during France's civil wars and dealing openly with men on both sides, telling each what he would tell the other.

fork.setup: you're Montaigne. civil war is on the roads, and every neighbor is fortifying. what do you do with your gate?
options: leave it open, with only a porter.
fork.reveal: he kept it open. a guarded house, he reasons, looks like a prize; his stayed unguarded, and he says it was spared.

trapdoor: what you thought: talking to both sides means having no side.
what it means: Montaigne kept his own side, said the same plain words to both, and paid for it in suspicion.
what a scholar hears: his open-gate passage, his candle for the saint and the dragon, and his complaint of being suspected by both camps come from three different essays, 2.15, 3.1 and 3.12.
recall: a try, a test, an attempt

sources.ref: Essays 2.15, That our desire is increased by difficulty (his house left unguarded during the civil wars, with only a porter)
Essays 3.1, Of the useful and the honest (dealing openly between princes; a candle to Saint Michael and one to his dragon)
Essays 3.12, Of physiognomy (moderation made him suspect to both parties)

notes: All Montaigne passages paraphrased. Confirm each attribution: open house (2.15), candle to Saint Michael and his dragon (3.1), suspected by both sides as Guelph to the Ghibellines and Ghibelline to the Guelphs (3.12).
The 'candle' line in 3.1 is said with irony and in a particular context; confirm the gloss 'he held to his own side, but refused to treat the other as monsters beyond reason' is fair.
'A round tower' and 'south of France' are general descriptions of his estate; the tower library is described in Essays 3.3. Cut if the claims editor wants only the text.
No dates, numbers of wars or names of princes given, by design.

Editor pass: re-glossed the candle line to match 3.1 (he follows his side to the fire but not into it), replacing a reading the text doesn't support; cut 'south of France', 'round' and 'both call their cause God's' (not in the cited essays); 'send for him to carry messages' softened to 'use him to carry word'; porter 'for custom and ceremony' per 2.15.
